rationale: Both responses are well structured and get the core ideas right: task-level success, position sweeps, synthetic probes to separate retrieval from reasoning, attention-mass audits, and tail and cascade pitfalls. Both also get the sample-size arithmetic wrong, since detecting 3 pp needs far more than 250-400 trials unless the design is paired. B is the stronger design overall. It gives an explicit 2D grid with an interaction test and a regression on real tasks with interaction terms. It adds a KL-divergence diagnostic, per-layer and per-head sensitivity, paired same-seed comparisons, exact details of the quantization scheme (K vs V, granularity, outliers), the interaction between weight and KV quantization, and version pinning. It also does a realistic feasibility check on a single host, with screening and prefix-caching mitigations. B has flaws: the compounding example labels success rates as failure rates, and its KV memory arithmetic ignores GQA. A has a structural weakness: its main baseline uses truncated FP16 context, which builds in the length confound it later flags. A also contains questionable claims, such as early tokens accumulating more quantization error, and its statement that failures on pure-reasoning probes rule out quantization as the cause is wrong. Its sample-size totals are internally inconsistent. On balance B is deeper, more actionable and better calibrated.
